analysis.one_liner: Speeds federal permits for new oil refineries, loosens Clean Air Act review, and pays refiners' delay costs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in any committee and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007, despite 37 Republican sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after Hurricane Katrina knocked out Gulf Coast refineries and pushed gas prices above $3 a gallon, the bill would have forced federal environmental and permitting agencies to approve refinery permits within 90 days, with the Energy Department issuing the permit itself if agencies missed the deadline. It would have created an Energy Department office to advocate for refinery applicants, sent federal lawyers to defend refiners against lawsuits over projects, and paid up to $500 million per facility out of a federal account for delays caused by litigation or agency slow-downs. It also would have relaxed Clean Air Act rules so that replacing polluting equipment would not trigger tougher pollution review, and would have barred states from keeping stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil refining companies gain the most: automatic permit approvals under eight environmental laws, a federal office advocating for their applications, free federal legal defense against lawsuits, federal payment of up to $500 million per new facility for costs caused by litigation or agency delays (including interest on their own debt), and looser equipment-replacement rules under the Clean Air Act. Small refiners get discounted crude oil from federal royalty supplies, up to $4.50 per barrel. Consumers benefit only indirectly, through the promise that more refining capacity would ease fuel prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil refiners, especially large new-plant sponsors

how_it_helps.text: Refinery permit applications under eight major environmental laws must be approved within 90 days, and if agencies miss the deadline the Secretary of Energy issues the permit directly [S3].

The Secretary of Energy would pay up to $500 million per contract for the first two qualifying new refineries, covering costs from litigation or agency review delays, including principal and interest on the sponsor's own debt [S3].
The Department of Energy would provide direct federal legal representation to refinery applicants sued over a permit or project, if the Secretary believes the lawsuit is a delay tactic [S3].
New Source Review under the Clean Air Act would treat equipment replacement as routine repair if emissions rise no more than 5% or 40 tons per year, and no state could adopt stricter rules [S3].

The bill's sponsors cited a real supply problem: no new refinery since 1976, refining capacity near 95% utilization, and a 4-million-barrel-per-day gap between capacity and demand filled by imports [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of the standby support program and federal legal defense for refiners, since the bill authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' in appropriations. People living near refineries would face weaker pollution review, because routine-exception equipment replacements would no longer trigger New Source Review and states could not impose stricter rules. Federal environmental agencies lose their leverage: a missed deadline means the permit is issued anyway.

drawbacks.text: The 90-day automatic approval covers permits under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, Superfund, and other laws, meaning an incomplete agency review ends with the permit being issued anyway; a presidential waiver is the only escape hatch, and a decision not to use it cannot be challenged in court [S3].

The standby support program shifts private business risk to taxpayers: the government would cover a sponsor's debt principal and interest and the cost of replacement fuel supplies when litigation or agency review delays a project, up to $500 million for each of the first two facilities and $250 million for four more [S3].

The Clean Air Act amendment is a floor, not just a ceiling: no state could include New Source Review provisions stricter than the federal rule in its implementation plan, stripping states of authority they currently hold [S3].

The Department of Energy would simultaneously advocate for applicants, push agencies to approve, and issue permits itself when deadlines lapse — the same office that promotes a project would also decide it, replacing independent review [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying problem was real: refining capacity was strained, prices spiked after Katrina, and the bill's findings are backed by the record. But almost every tool in the bill transfers money or legal power to refiners directly — delay insurance, free federal lawyers, an in-house advocacy office, and automatic permits — while the benefit to drivers runs only through the hope that new capacity eventually lowers prices. The Clean Air Act rollback and the ban on stricter state rules impose real pollution and oversight costs with no guaranteed price payoff. A narrower bill aimed purely at permitting timelines would have carried far less of the industry subsidy.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then two subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Shadegg and 36 Republican cosponsors introduced the bill on September 20, 2005, three weeks after Hurricane Katrina disrupted Gulf refining and sent gasoline above $3 a gallon nationally [S3][S4].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Resources, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees on the day of introduction [S5].
The following two days, it was referred to the Water Resources and Environment subcommittee and the Energy and Air Quality subcommittee; the record shows no further action of any kind [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and all legislation not enacted died, including this bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Refining companies never got the permit deadlines, federal delay insurance, free legal defense, or the Clean Air Act rollback they sought. Existing environmental review requirements and state authority stayed intact, and taxpayer dollars were never committed to the program — though the country also got no new refining capacity from this effort.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Air rules and federal funds stayed intact

for.name: Rep. John Shadegg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 20, 2005, framing it as a response to the post-Katrina fuel supply crisis

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 20, 2005, and sent it to the Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote

against.name: House Natural Resources and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Received referrals and took no recorded action on the bill

sides.party_line_note: All 37 supporters — Shadegg plus 36 cosponsors — were Republicans, and no Democrat cosponsored; the bill never reached a floor vote where any partisan split could be recorded.

industries.note: The bill hands refiners automatic 90-day permits, a federal advocacy office, free federal legal defense, and up to $500 million per facility in taxpayer-funded delay coverage, while loosening the Clean Air Act rules that govern their plants. The public benefit — more fuel supply and possibly lower prices — is indirect and uncertain, while the pollution review and fiscal costs are direct.
Qualifying small refineries could buy federal royalty crude at a discount of up to $4.50 per barrel, a direct subsidy from public mineral revenues to a private industry.

industries.industry: Communities near refineries and environmental regulators
industries.note: Weaker New Source Review rules and a ban on stricter state provisions would reduce the pollution oversight that shields nearby residents.
